Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the stream `orders`; the consumer group comes from the broker. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place)) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the stream `orders`; the consumer group comes from the broker. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build())) }

A slice handler reads one XREADGROUP COUNT on a stream; a list or a channel builds its batch on the client up to the same size. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The step is required on a slice handler: mounting one without it does not compile. A single-message handler does not offer the step at all; its concurrency is workers(n). On a stream the size is the COUNT of the read that fetches the batch, XREADGROUP or XAUTOCLAIM. The server sends at most n entries, and the handler gets exactly what one read returned, never an empty batch. A list and a channel deliver one value at a time. Their subscriptions gather a batch on the client from the values already waiting, up to the same n, and hand it over without waiting for more. So a batch is often smaller than n, and a quiet key yields batches of one. One outcome settles every entry of the batch. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) settles the batch with an ack and Err(outcomes) settles entry i with outcome i. A stream batch reads a StreamBatchContext, which carries the group and its seek handle and no field of one entry. The block step chains after the size.

Three values waiting on each form arrive in one call. The stream handler and the app: Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Bills the orders one read returned, at most 16. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"))] async fn bill(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(bill.batch(nonzero!(16))) .include(pack.batch(nonzero!(16))) .include(count.batch(nonzero!(16))) }) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Bills the orders one read returned. struct Bill; impl Handle<[Order]> for Bill { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Bill).batch(nonzero!(16)).build()) .include( subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs"), Pack) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build(), ) .include( subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("clicks"), Count) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build(), ) }) } The list and the channel handlers: Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Packs the jobs waiting on the list `jobs`, at most 16 at once. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs"))] async fn pack(jobs: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Counts the clicks heard on the channel `clicks`, at most 16 at once. #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("clicks"))] async fn count(clicks: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Packs the jobs waiting on the list `jobs`. struct Pack; impl Handle<[Order]> for Pack { fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs packed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Counts the clicks heard on the channel `clicks`. struct Count; impl Handle<[Order]> for Count { fn handle( &self, clicks: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks counted"); ready(Ok(())) } }

block sets how long one read waits on the server: the XREADGROUP BLOCK on a stream, the BRPOP or BLMOVE timeout on a list. The wait is five seconds unless a subscription names another. A descriptor names it with RedisStream::block or RedisList::block. The mount site names it with the block step, which overrides the descriptor. The step chains after another step of the mount chain: after .batch(n), after .pipeline(), or, in the manual form, after build(). It reads the same before and after start_at(..). On a reclaim subscription the wait is the pause between two XAUTOCLAIM scans that found nothing. A read wakes as soon as an entry arrives, so the wait costs nothing on a busy stream. It decides how soon an idle read sees what happens beside it: a seek of its group, or a due entry of a delay queue, which the subscription sweeps once per read. A shorter wait sees them sooner, at the price of one more round trip per idle wait. The step exists on stream and list subscriptions, the two forms whose read blocks.

Orders wait at most a second per read; invoices are billed sixteen at a time, with a two-second wait set at the mount site. Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_block.rs /// Each read of `orders` waits at most one second on the server. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers").block(Duration::from_secs(1)))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Bills up to 16 orders a read. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("invoices").group("billing"))] async fn bill(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place) // The size is the framework's step and the wait is Redis's, chained after it. .include(bill.batch(nonzero!(16)).block(Duration::from_secs(2))) }) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_block.rs /// Places one order. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Bills the orders of one read. struct Bill; impl Handle<[Order]> for Bill { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Each read of `orders` waits at most one second on the server. let orders = RedisStream::new("orders") .group("workers") .block(Duration::from_secs(1)); let invoices = RedisStream::new("invoices").group("billing"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Place).build()).include( subscriber(invoices, Bill) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build() .block(Duration::from_secs(2)), ) }) }

An envelope is how a message's headers travel beside its payload; the broker names one, and a descriptor or a publish policy names its own. A list element and a channel message are one value, and a stream entry is a map of fields. An envelope is the layout of the headers and the payload in them. RedisBroker::envelope sets the broker's envelope, and every subscription and publish policy uses it unless it names its own. A subscription names its own at the mount site with RedisEnvelopeExt::envelope: b.include(handler.envelope(FastStream)). On the manual path the descriptor names it: RedisList::new("jobs").envelope(FastStream). A publish policy names its own with envelope(..): RedisListPublish::new().envelope(FastStream). The envelope is a type, so the choice costs nothing per message. A delivery finds its payload without reading the headers, and reads them the first time a handler asks. A header block that does not parse reads as no headers, and the subscription logs a warning; a handler that requires a header then meets the ordinary missing-header error. Envelope List element, channel message Stream entry envelope::RustStream, the default a binary frame that opens with a marker; a message without headers is its bare payload the payload in _payload, each header in h:<name> FastStream faststream's BinaryMessageFormatV1 the same frame in __data__ Framed a {headers, payload} document written by a codec, its payload in CloudEvents' convention the document in _payload NoOp the payload alone the payload in _payload envelope::RustStream writes the bytes every earlier release wrote, so services on different releases read each other. A binary frame written by 0.7.1 or an earlier release has no marker and reads as its payload, frame bytes included, so services that share a list or a channel upgrade together. FastStream shares lists, channels and streams with a faststream service in both directions. Its header names travel as they are, so faststream's own headers arrive as correlation_id and reply_to. Framed with JsonCodec writes text that redis-cli and RedisInsight show as it is. Its payload follows the convention of CloudEvents' JSON format. A payload that is a JSON text is embedded as the value it is and reads back byte for byte: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload":{"id":7}}. Any other payload travels as standard base64: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload_base64":"CAc="}. With CBOR, msgpack or a codec of the service's own the payload is a byte string in payload; the codec implements FrameCodec, which this crate's json, cbor and msgpack features do for the framework's codecs. A header is a text field, and a header whose value is not text refuses the publish. The document of the codec(..) framing of 0.7.2 and earlier releases carried its payload as a string, so Framed reads it as a JSON string; services that share such a list switch together, and the list is drained first. A value that is not one of the envelope's own arrives as the payload with no headers, whatever its first bytes are. A stream entry without the envelope's field arrives as one JSON object of its fields. A payload that only looks like an envelope is written so that it reads back unchanged. A subscription and the publishers that write its name use one envelope. The broker's default publisher, which writes a retry copy and a reply that name no policy, writes the broker's envelope and the built-in ones. A subscription that reads through an envelope of the service's own, on a broker with another one, has its retry copies published through a policy that names it, out_retry(Publish::new().envelope(MyEnvelope)); the default publisher refuses that name, and the error names it. Two subscriptions that read one name through different envelopes stop the service at startup. NoOp has no room for headers, so a delivery read through it carries none of the message's. The headers a stream read itself reports, the delivery count and the idle time of a claiming read, stay. A publish through it that carries a header fails, and the error names the header and the destination. A retry copy the runtime publishes carries its retry count in a header, so a retry through NoOp fails the same way.

A faststream shop appends orders to a stream, and the broker reads its frame. Jobs go to a list as JSON documents, and a price feed publishes bare JSON. Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_envelopes.rs /// The list jobs leave through. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Job)] struct Jobs; /// Reads the orders a faststream shop appends, in the broker's envelope, and queues a job for /// each with the tenant in a header. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("dispatch"))] async fn dispatch(order: &Order, Out(jobs): Out<impl Publisher, Jobs>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("tenant", order.tenant.clone()); let job = Job { order: order.id }; if jobs .message(&job) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Runs each job for the tenant its header names; the list holds JSON documents. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs"))] async fn run(job: &Job, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") else { tracing::warn!(job.order, "a job without a tenant is dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; tracing::info!(job.order, tenant, "job run"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads the prices a feed publishes as bare JSON, with no headers. #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices"))] async fn on_price(price: &Price) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(price.sku, price.cents, "price"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // faststream's frame wherever nothing names another envelope. let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").envelope(FastStream); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Both ends of `jobs` name JSON, so `redis-cli` and RedisInsight show each job as text. b.include(dispatch) .out( Jobs, RedisListPublish::new().envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec)), ) .build() .include(run.envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))) .include(on_price.envelope(NoOp)) }) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_envelopes.rs /// The list jobs leave through. struct Jobs; impl OutSlot for Jobs { const NAME: &'static str = "Jobs"; // `Job` fixes its destination, so no transform on this slot may name one. type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Jobs> for Job {} /// Reads the orders a faststream shop appends, in the broker's envelope, and queues a job for /// each with the tenant in a header. struct Dispatch; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Dispatch where Entry: OutEntry<Jobs, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("tenant", order.tenant.clone()); let job = Job { order: order.id }; outs.get(Jobs) .message(&job) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } /// Runs each job for the tenant its header names; the list holds JSON documents. struct Run; impl Handle<Job> for Run { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") else { tracing::warn!(job.order, "a job without a tenant is dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); }; tracing::info!(job.order, tenant, "job run"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Reads the prices a feed publishes as bare JSON, with no headers. struct OnPrice; impl Handle<Price> for OnPrice { fn handle( &self, price: &Price, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(price.sku, price.cents, "price"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // faststream's frame wherever nothing names another envelope. let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").envelope(FastStream); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("dispatch"); let jobs = RedisList::new("jobs").envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec)); let prices = RedisPubSub::new("prices").envelope(NoOp); // Both ends of `jobs` name JSON, so `redis-cli` and RedisInsight show each job as text. b.include(subscriber(orders, Dispatch).build()) .out( Jobs, RedisListPublish::new().envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec)), ) .build() .include(subscriber(jobs, Run).build()) .include(subscriber(prices, OnPrice).build()) }) }

An envelope of the service's own implements Envelope. locate finds the payload in a value, headers reads the headers, and seal writes a message. A stream entry keeps the sealed value in _payload unless the envelope overrides entry_field or the other entry methods. A broker whose own envelope is one of the service's own, or Framed over a codec of the service's, registers itself with the test harness beside the tests: ruststream::register_testable_broker!(RedisBroker<MyEnvelope>);. Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_envelopes.rs /// One JSON line with the headers under `meta` and the payload as text under `body`: the layout /// a legacy system on the same list writes. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] struct MetaLine; #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Line { meta: BTreeMap<String, String>, body: String, } impl Envelope for MetaLine { const CONTENT_TYPE: &'static str = "application/json"; fn locate(&self, value: &[u8]) -> Location { serde_json::from_slice::<Line>(value).map_or(Location::Bare, |line| { Location::Decoded(line.body.into_bytes()) }) } fn headers(&self, value: &[u8]) -> Option<HeaderMap> { let line = serde_json::from_slice::<Line>(value).ok()?; let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); for (name, text) in line.meta { headers.insert(name, text); } Some(headers) } fn seal( &self, payload: &[u8], headers: &HeaderMap, value: &mut Vec<u8>, ) -> Result<(), SealError> { let line = Line { meta: headers .iter() .map(|(name, text)| (name.to_owned(), String::from_utf8_lossy(text).into_owned())) .collect(), body: String::from_utf8_lossy(payload).into_owned(), }; serde_json::to_writer(value, &line).map_err(|err| SealError::Encode(Box::new(err))) } } /// Reads the legacy system's lines, the tenant from `meta`. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("legacy.jobs"))] async fn legacy(job: &LegacyJob, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or("unknown"); tracing::info!(job.order, tenant, "legacy job run"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn legacy_app() -> impl App { // The legacy system's layout is the envelope of the whole broker. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("legacy", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").envelope(MetaLine), |b| b.include(legacy), ) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_envelopes.rs /// One JSON line with the headers under `meta` and the payload as text under `body`: the layout /// a legacy system on the same list writes. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] struct MetaLine; #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Line { meta: BTreeMap<String, String>, body: String, } impl Envelope for MetaLine { const CONTENT_TYPE: &'static str = "application/json"; fn locate(&self, value: &[u8]) -> Location { serde_json::from_slice::<Line>(value).map_or(Location::Bare, |line| { Location::Decoded(line.body.into_bytes()) }) } fn headers(&self, value: &[u8]) -> Option<HeaderMap> { let line = serde_json::from_slice::<Line>(value).ok()?; let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); for (name, text) in line.meta { headers.insert(name, text); } Some(headers) } fn seal( &self, payload: &[u8], headers: &HeaderMap, value: &mut Vec<u8>, ) -> Result<(), SealError> { let line = Line { meta: headers .iter() .map(|(name, text)| (name.to_owned(), String::from_utf8_lossy(text).into_owned())) .collect(), body: String::from_utf8_lossy(payload).into_owned(), }; serde_json::to_writer(value, &line).map_err(|err| SealError::Encode(Box::new(err))) } } /// Reads the legacy system's lines, the tenant from `meta`. struct Legacy; impl Handle<LegacyJob> for Legacy { fn handle( &self, job: &LegacyJob, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or("unknown"); tracing::info!(job.order, tenant, "legacy job run"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn legacy_app() -> impl App { // The legacy system's layout is the envelope of the whole broker. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("legacy", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").envelope(MetaLine), |b| { let jobs = RedisList::new("legacy.jobs"); b.include(subscriber(jobs, Legacy).build()) }, ) }

TestApp::start runs the service's app on RedisBroker connected to a Redis modelled in process, groups, lists and channels included. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<RedisBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The connected broker is the production one. Every command it sends, a publish, a group read, an acknowledgement, a delay-queue sweep, reaches the model as that command and is answered as Redis answers it. The model reads every setting off the broker. Its address is parsed as the connect parses it, and the pool size, the default group and the cluster topology carry over. It answers as Redis 8.4, so a claiming subscription mounts. It keeps key types: a write or a read of the wrong type fails with WRONGTYPE. It keeps consumer groups with their cursor, pending entries and delivery counts, the group's start_id, XAUTOCLAIM and XREADGROUP ... CLAIM at their idle thresholds, and a seek. It keeps lists with the processing list and its recovery set, sorted sets, key expiry and MULTI / EXEC. Pub/Sub channels, globs and sharded channels deliver to the subscriptions open at that moment and store nothing for one that is not. On a cluster topology it refuses a command or a transaction that spans hash slots. It runs no scripts: EVAL, EVALSHA, FCALL and a command it does not know fail with an error naming them. No handshake runs, so AUTH, HELLO and TLS are for a live test. A test's input goes where the default publisher writes its name: an XADD, or the LPUSH or PUBLISH of the subscription that reads the name. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply included, so the assertions that follow read finished state. published::<T>(name) reads every write to the name back, a requeued copy and an entry a delay queue adds back included. The model's time is the test's clock: entry ids, idle times and the scores of the delay queue and the recovery set stand still on a paused clock, and tb.advance(by) moves them. A handler's own commands, through FredPool or a pipeline window, reach the model too.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it.
